content: Polystyrene sulfonate is an electrolyte medication approved by the FDA for the treatment of hyperkalemia. Common adverse reactions include fecal impaction and ischemic colitis. Adult Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications and Dosage (Adult): Polystyrene sulfonate is indicated for the treatment of hyperkalemia. The average daily adult dose ranges from 15 g (60 mL) to 60 g (240 mL) of suspension. This is typically administered as 15 g (60 mL) of SPS® Suspension one to four times daily. Each 60 mL of SPS® Suspension contains 1500 mg (65 mEq) of sodium. Due to the in-vivo efficiency of sodium-potassium exchange resins being approximately 33%, about one-third of the resin’s sodium content is delivered to the body. In smaller children and infants, lower doses should be calculated based on a rate of 1 mEq of potassium per gram of resin. SPS® Suspension can be introduced into the stomach via a plastic tube and may be given with a diet suitable for patients with renal failure. Alternatively, it can be administered rectally as an enema, though this method is less effective. For adults, the enema dose is 30 g (120 mL) to 50 g (200 mL) every six hours. The enema should be retained as long as possible and followed by a cleansing enema. After an initial cleansing enema, a soft, large-size (French 28) rubber tube is inserted into the rectum to a depth of about 20 cm, with the tip positioned in the sigmoid colon. The suspension is introduced at body temperature by gravity, flushed with 50–100 mL of fluid, and the tube is clamped and left in place. If back leakage occurs, the hips should be elevated on pillows or the patient should assume a knee-chest position temporarily. The suspension should remain in the sigmoid colon for several hours, if possible. The colon is then irrigated with a sodium-free cleansing enema at body temperature to remove the resin. Up to two quarts of flushing solution may be required. The returns are drained continuously through a Y-tube connection. Special attention should be given to the cleansing enema, as sorbitol is present in the vehicle. The intensity and duration of therapy depend on the severity and resistance of hyperkalemia. SPS® Suspension should not be heated, as this may alter the resin’s exchange properties. Off-Label Use and Dosage (Adult): There is limited information regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use of polystyrene sulfonate in adults. Pediatric Indications and Dosage FDA-Labeled Indications and Dosage (Pediatric): Limited information is available regarding FDA-labeled use of polystyrene sulfonate in pediatric patients. Off-Label Use and Dosage (Pediatric): Limited information is available regarding off-label guideline-supported or non-guideline-supported use of polystyrene sulfonate in pediatric patients. Contraindications SPS® Suspension is contraindicated in patients with hypokalemia, a history of hypersensitivity to polystyrene sulfonate resins, obstructive bowel disease, and in neonates for oral or rectal administration. Warnings Cases of intestinal necrosis, which may be fatal, and other serious gastrointestinal adverse events (e.g., bleeding, ischemic colitis, perforation) have been reported with sodium polystyrene sulfonate use. Most cases involved concomitant use of sorbitol. Risk factors include prematurity, a history of intestinal disease or surgery, hypovolemia, and renal insufficiency or failure. Concomitant administration of additional sorbitol is not recommended. Use only in patients with normal bowel function. Avoid use in patients who have not had a bowel movement post-surgery. Avoid use in patients at risk for constipation or impaction, including those with a history of impaction, chronic constipation, inflammatory bowel disease, ischemic colitis, vascular intestinal atherosclerosis, previous bowel resection, or bowel obstruction. Discontinue use in patients who develop constipation. Severe hyperkalemia may constitute a medical emergency, necessitating definitive measures such as dialysis. Serious potassium deficiency can occur with sodium polystyrene sulfonate therapy. Frequent serum potassium monitoring (every 24 hours) is essential. Intracellular potassium deficiency may not always be reflected by serum potassium levels, so treatment discontinuation thresholds must be individualized based on clinical condition and electrocardiogram findings. Severe hypokalemia may present with irritability, confusion, delayed thought processes, muscle weakness, paralysis, or apnea. Electrocardiographic changes may include a prolonged QT interval, T wave flattening or inversion, and prominent U waves. Cardiac arrhythmias, such as premature atrial, nodal, and ventricular contractions, and tachycardias, may occur. Digitalis toxicity may be exaggerated. Marked hypokalemia may also manifest as severe muscle weakness or paralysis. Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not entirely selective for potassium and may cause losses of magnesium and calcium. Patients should be monitored for all applicable electrolyte disturbances. Systemic alkalosis has been reported when cation-exchange resins were administered orally with nonabsorbable cation-donating antacids and laxatives (e.g., magnesium hydroxide, aluminum carbonate). Magnesium hydroxide should not be co-administered with sodium polystyrene sulfonate. One case of grand mal seizure was reported in a patient with chronic hypocalcemia of renal failure who received sodium polystyrene sulfonate with magnesium hydroxide as a laxative. Adverse Reactions Clinical Trials Experience: Limited information is available regarding clinical trial experience with polystyrene sulfonate. Postmarketing Experience: SPS® Suspension may cause gastric irritation, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, and constipation, particularly at high doses. Hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, hypomagnesemia, and significant sodium retention, along with their related clinical manifestations, may occur. Diarrhea may occasionally develop. Large doses in elderly individuals may cause fecal impaction. Rare cases of intestinal necrosis have been reported. Intestinal obstruction due to aluminum hydroxide concretions, when used with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, has been reported. Other reported events include fecal impaction following rectal administration (especially in children), gastrointestinal concretions (bezoars) following oral administration, ischemic colitis, gastrointestinal tract ulceration or necrosis leading to intestinal perforation, and rare cases of acute bronchitis or bronchopneumonia associated with inhalation of polystyrene sulfonate particles. Drug Interactions Limited information is available regarding drug interactions with polystyrene sulfonate. Use in Specific Populations Pregnancy: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is classified as Pregnancy Category C by the FDA. Animal reproduction studies have not been conducted, and it is unknown whether the drug can cause fetal harm or affect reproductive capacity. It should only be used during pregnancy if clearly needed. There is no Australian Drug Evaluation Committee (ADEC) guidance on its use in pregnant women. Labor and Delivery: No FDA guidance is available on its use during labor and delivery. Nursing Mothers: It is unknown whether this drug is excreted in human milk. Caution should be exercised when administering sodium polystyrene sulfonate to nursing women. Pediatric Use: The effectiveness of SPS® Suspension in pediatric patients has not been established. Its use is contraindicated in neonates, particularly premature infants. Rectal administration in children and neonates requires caution, as excessive dosage may result in resin impaction. Adequate volumes of sodium-free cleansing enemas should be used after rectal administration. Geriatric Use: No FDA guidance is available regarding its use in geriatric patients. Gender, Race, Renal Impairment, Hepatic Impairment, and Immunocompromised Patients: No specific FDA guidance is available for these populations. Administration and Monitoring Administration: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate is not administered intravenously. Monitoring: Patients receiving sodium polystyrene sulfonate should be monitored for all applicable electrolyte disturbances. Overdosage Overdosage may result in electrolyte disturbances, including hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, and hypomagnesemia. Clinical signs of hypokalemia include irritability, confusion, delayed thought processes, muscle weakness, hyporeflexia, paralysis, and apnea. Tetany may occur. Electrocardiographic changes consistent with hypokalemia or hypocalcemia, as well as cardiac arrhythmias, may be observed. Appropriate measures should be taken to correct serum electrolytes (potassium, calcium, magnesium), and the resin should be removed from the alimentary tract using laxatives or enemas. Pharmacology Mechanism of Action: Sodium ions in the resin are partially released and replaced by potassium ions as the resin passes through the intestine or is retained in the colon after enema administration. This action primarily occurs in the large intestine, which excretes potassium ions more effectively than the small intestine. The efficiency of this process is limited and variable, commonly approximating 33%. Electrolyte balance must be closely monitored. Metabolic data are unavailable. How Supplied SPS® Suspension is a light brown, cherry-flavored suspension supplied in pint (473 mL), 120 mL, and 60 mL unit dose bottles. Dispense in a tight container as defined by the USP. If repackaged, store in a refrigerator and use within 14 days. Shake well before use. Storage Store at 25°C (77°F); excursions permitted to 15°–30°C (59°–86°F).
